In determining reasonableness 
or fairness, 
the primary concern 
must be with the terms of the contract considered 
in light of the 
circumstances 
existing when the contract was made. The test is not 
simple, nor can it be mechanically applied. The terms are to be considered 
"in the light of the general commercial background and the commercial 
needs of the particular trade or case."8 Corbin suggests the test as being 
whether the terms are "so extreme as to appear unconscionable according 
to the mores and business practices of the time and place." 1 Corbin, op. 
cit. supra Note 2.9 We think this formulation correctly states the test to 
be applied in those cases where no meaningful choice was exercised upon 
entering the contract. 
Because the trial court and the appellate 
court did not feel that 
enforcement could be refused, no findings were made on the possible 
unconscionability of the contracts in these cases. Since the record is not 
sufficient for our deciding the issue as a matter of law, the cases must be 
remanded to the trial court for further proceedings. 
So ordered.
